# Tamago

French learning app, installable web app, mobile first. React, Vite, Tailwind v4. Hosted on Cloudflare Pages (project tamago, https://tamago-83f.pages.dev), Git-connected: every push to main deploys (one site; the parked dev site is under Testing, One site). No backend except two Pages Functions, functions/api/explain.js and generate.js (handlers shared in server/; Claude explaining mistakes and Claude-written practice; both off until TAMAGO_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set as a Pages secret; never fall back to a generic ANTHROPIC_API_KEY). The service worker caches the page as / because Pages redirects /index.html. Netlify (tamago-590) is retired: builds stopped 2026-11-09, site kept at Dan's request, frozen at Phase 5; netlify/ and netlify.toml stay only as its record.

Specs are in `_source/`: tamago-feature-list.md (what), build-phases.md (order of work), question-types.md (question logic), tamago-data-v4.xlsx (all content; lesson_rules tab holds R01 to R16), learning-methods.md (why), tamago-phase0-decisions.xlsx (decision log).
The workbook is edited outside this repo and gets reissued. Never edit it here, and never write check results into it. A new version goes in `_source/` and becomes the default path in `scripts/import.mjs`.

## Working mode

From 2026-11-09 the build runs under `_source/autonomous-build.md`: phase by phase through build-phases.md, test, commit and push at each phase end, log to `_source/build-log.md`, and overwrite `_source/check-in.md` (Done, Decisions made, Waiting for Dan). Claude owns the workbook now: edit it in place, changelog row in README, bump the version each phase. Stop only for money or accounts, making it public, deleting Dan's files, and the native-speaker check.

## Team (Dan, 2026-11-15)

- Dan: the orchestrator. Routes work between sessions, tests, approves. Nothing goes public, costs money, creates accounts or deletes data without him.
- Planner: Claude in claude.ai, outside Claude Code. Writes specs and the pastes Dan brings here.
- Builder 1: the main builder. Owns main, the app code and merges.
- Builder 2: only when Dan starts one. Works in its own worktree and branch, content only, never merges. Framework needs go in a _review/ file for Builder 1.
- Fable: the judge. Reviews craft and content against the rubric and writes only to _review/. Never changes code, never switches branches in the main tree.
- Debugger: a fresh session for one bug at a time.
- Handoffs: through Dan's pastes. Every report ends with a Live/Not Done checklist, and no spreadsheets unless asked.
- Pushing: before every push, pull the latest main from GitHub, re-run the tests, and only then push. Never force-push. If a pull brings in changes to files you also changed, merge carefully and say so in your report.
- Testing (Dan, 2026-11-16, tiered): Testing is standard and doesn't need to be asked for. Every push: pull, then push; the pre-push hook runs the fast tier (`npm run test:fast`: every logic test, the whole-course content sweeps in full for the courses whose content changed since the last push, a fixed 5% sample of every other course) with the secrets, smoke and audio-stop checks. The full suite (`npm test`) runs in GitHub Actions after every push to main (.github/workflows/full-suite.yml) and reports failures; a failure there is fixed in the next push. Rebuild and audit only the courses whose content changed. If a new request arrives during a test run, finish the run and push first, then start the new request, unless it's urgent.

## Design system (Dan, 2026-11-19)

Rule for every builder: build screens from the components in COMPONENTS.md. A new shared piece goes into src/components/ with a story beside it and an entry in COMPONENTS.md. Never hand-write a duplicate of a component that exists; if one almost fits, extend it, or note the gap under "Duplicates to Settle" in COMPONENTS.md.

The app adopted the components with no visual change (branch design-system-adopt, made from design-system; proof in its handoff: the app's built CSS identical to main's, matching screenshots, no Konsta UI or Storybook in the bundle). The iOS and Android styles are Storybook only. How it was built, step by step, on branch `design-system` (worktree Sites/tamago-design-system), which stays as the place for proposals: Storybook 10 (`npm run storybook`, http://localhost:6006/; .storybook/ with its own small Vite config, telemetry off, src/index.css loaded, toolbar Theme light/dark and sizes Phone 390 px and Desktop 1440 px). Lifted unchanged into src/components/: ChoiceList and AnswerBar (from Lesson.jsx, which still exports AnswerBar for test/lesson-ui.test.js), Sheet with SheetHead (from Home.jsx), and WrongMark (ChoiceList needs it); LISTENING moved to src/lib/question-names.js. Stories sit beside each component (*.stories.jsx; explain.js is mocked in .storybook/preview.jsx so no story calls the server); the docs page is src/components/DesignSystemCard.mdx; COMPONENTS.md lists every component. Stories use only classes the app already uses, so the app's built CSS is unchanged. Step 2 (same day): Button (kinds main, continue, outline, link = btn-submit, btn-primary, btn-secondary, btn-tertiary, whose names stay; used on the question page only, the other buttons left as they are, Dan's call), ProgressBar, QuestionHeading (takes `part`; Lesson.jsx keeps partOf), SentenceText (FrenchText, FirstSight), LevelLine (was Home's Marker), ToolTile (ToolPill, ToolCard, TOOL_ICONS), Toast lifted; CircleNode, AudioHelp, Logo and FlagRow (was screens/Languages.jsx) moved from src/screens to src/components with git mv, importers updated; icons.jsx stays in src/screens. test/lesson-ui.test.js's logo test reads both folders. Storybook also has Colors (reads src/index.css itself), Type and Spacing (counts as of 2026-11-19, src/components/docs/) and Icons pages; audio.js is watched (sb.mock spy) so AudioHelp stories are silent; staticDirs is public/. Docs helpers use inline styles, not new classes. Step 3 (same day), iOS and Android styles, Storybook only: konsta 5.5.0 and @fontsource-variable/roboto are dev dependencies; the app never imports either. src/components/style/StyleContext.jsx (StyleProvider, useStyle, usePlatformPart; no provider = 'tamago', so the app is unchanged); Button, ProgressBar, Toast, ChoiceList, ToolPill and Sheet hand over to src/components/platform/* (Konsta components in Tamago's colors) when a platform style is on; every other component stays Tamago's and is adapted by .storybook/platform.css under .k-ios / .k-material, found through data-ds attributes. platform.css builds Konsta's classes in their own `konsta` layer, below the app's utilities, and must be imported before src/index.css in .storybook/preview.jsx (else Konsta's plain classes beat the app's lg: ones). Toolbar: Style (Tamago, iOS, Android) beside Theme and size. The Tamago style must stay pixel-identical: compare story screenshots before and after any change here. Stories and platform files must not introduce Tailwind classes the app lacks (the app's built CSS must stay byte-identical); use the tg-* classes in platform.css instead. Step 4 (same day), two screens in Storybook under Screens: src/components/screens/QuestionPage.jsx (Pick the Meaning) and MainPage.jsx, built from library components only, sample content in screens/sample.js, no network; Compare.jsx draws one story in the three styles in iframes (phone side by side, desktop stacked by default). Lifted from Home.jsx for them: TopBar, ToolStrip and ToolPanel (in ToolTile.jsx), PinnedAction; new: IconButton. Platform parts added: TopBar (Konsta Navbar), ToolStrip (Konsta Tabbar: Learn, three tools, More), PinnedAction (iOS Button above the tab bar, Android Konsta Fab). Proposed look changes are not here: the phone layout of the circle's two icons (above the circle like ears, smaller, quieter) lives on branch design-system and its published Storybook only, listed on the Design System Card under "Proposed, Not in the App". Published copy (Dan, 2026-11-19): https://dgbenner.github.io/tamago-design-system/, the built Storybook only, on the gh-pages branch of the public repo dgbenner/tamago-design-system; `npm run publish-storybook` (scripts/publish-storybook.sh, which runs on branch design-system only, since the published copy shows the proposals too: build, gitleaks with scripts/publish-gitleaks.toml, checks for personal paths, recordings and server names, a normal commit on top of gh-pages, never the design-system branch). ## Content pipeline

`npm run content` runs three steps (`npm run pull` proposes sentences for draft units; `content/drafts.json` holds drafted sentences; decisions also carry cut_sentences, vocabulary_additions, hints and borrow until the workbook absorbs them):

1. `import`: workbook to `content/raw/`. Fails on broken IDs. Also validates sentence_words, pairs, round_type_mix, phase1_fallbacks and cant_swaps.
2. `check`: Tatoeba, Wiktionary and Lingua Libre to `content/checks/` and `content/review.md`. Generates the en_to_fr answers (workbook README). Downloads are cached in `.cache/`.
3. `build:content`: writes `src/content/`, bundled into the app, and copies recordings to `public/audio/`. The workbook's status is the gate, and the build fails if the checks disagree with it.

A1 stoplist (Dan, 2026-11-20; standing step for every course): scripts/lib/a1-stoplist.mjs lists words no A1 list may count (oaths, slurs, violence, subtitle leftovers such as English words and names, official register), shared (ALL) and per course. build-content drops them from the shipped a1_list (so the app's "% of A1 words" leaves them out) and writes what it dropped to content*/a1-dropped.json; a1-coverage leaves them out of the target. Started from Italian's register cuts (also in content-it/a1-exclude.json) and Dutch's 31; Danish 35 and Norwegian 31 added. A new language adds its own junk under its key and logs it; nobody is asked. Nothing stops a word being taught.

Form-of hints (2026-11-22, every course; Fable's phase 6 reviews found Swedish 136, Danish 163, Dutch 39 hints that were a bare label such as "present of kunne"): scripts/lib/form-of.mjs bareFormOf recognises a definition that is only a form-of label and its word ("present of kunne", "past participle of doen", "comparative degree of oud", "alternative spelling of i morgon", optionally with Wiktionary's quoted gloss). check-content then reads that word's own Wiktionary entry through its usual cached code (first gloss under the same part of speech, a participle's under Verb, skipping glosses that are labels themselves; lemma_match in word-senses.json picks another sense) and stores it as lemma_gloss; the word's lemma is left as it was, so a comparative still counts as itself on the A1 list. build-content's hintFrom makes the hint "meaning (label)": "to be able, can (present of kunne)". Hints from review decisions or claude_hints still win, and the older "person/plural/singular/inflection" rule ("cat (kot)") runs first and is unchanged. A wrong meaning is fixed with lemma_match or a hint decision, never by editing the built file.

US spelling (2026-11-22, every course; was colour only): scripts/lib/us-spelling.mjs UK_US lists every UK spelling found in the shipped English (Fable's lists plus a scan of all courses: Mum, theatre, centre, metre, litre, harbour, neighbour(hood), favourite, flavour, behaviour, travelling, cancelled, programme, practise, apologise, organise, recognise, licence, grey, aeroplane, maths, storey and more). build-content applies it through usSpellingTable to each table's English fields only (ENGLISH in that file: sentences.english, word glosses and hints, notes and overview lines, part summaries, task items, reading-text questions, prompts, can-do statements, English feedback lines), leaving **bold** course-language words inside them alone; every other string gets the old colour-only rule. The course language (french column, forms, lemmas, reading texts, form cards) is never respelled. A gloss that gave both spellings keeps one ("neighbor", not "neighbor, neighbor"). Accepted answers are not respelled; equivalents.mjs adds each UK/US pair both ways (not check, story, tire, which have other meanings). test/us-spelling.test.js fails if any UK spelling from the list is in any course's shipped English. A new UK word goes into UK_US.

# Tamago: craft review

Draft 1, November 9, 2026. For a separate reviewer: a fresh Claude Code session that did not build Tamago.
It grades how the app looks and feels, not the French content or the learning logic.

## How to run it

1. Open the live site in a desktop browser at 1280 px wide. Do a phone pass at 390 px only when Dan asks.
2. Use it as a new learner: home, one full lesson in Unit 1 round 1, one lesson in a later unit and round, a
   missed answer, Review, Words, Verbs, Settings, and both light and dark mode.
3. Take a screenshot of every distinct screen and state. Save them in `_review/<date>/`.
4. Time it: seconds from Continue to the next question, and the total time for one lesson.
5. Grade each criterion below from 1 to 5. Write one line of evidence for each grade, naming the screenshot.
6. List fixes, most important first: what's wrong, where (screenshot), the fix, and which criterion it lifts.
7. Write it all to `_review/<date>/craft-review.md`. Change no code. The builder makes the fixes afterward.

Grade honestly. A 5 is rare. When in doubt between two grades, give the lower one.

## Criteria

**1. No dead time.** Every second in a lesson goes to questions.
- 5: The next question appears at once. No loading screens, celebrations or animations hold the learner. A lesson
  takes about 10 minutes or less.
- 3: Small waits or extra taps between questions, or one screen to click through after the lesson.
- 1: Spinners, transitions or screens that hold the learner.

**2. One thing on screen.** While answering, the screen shows the question and its answer controls, nothing else.
- 5: Nothing competes with the question. Flag and comment appear only in the answer bar.
- 3: Some extra elements (counters, labels, decoration) take attention.
- 1: The question fights with other content.

**3. Obvious in one second.** A learner knows what to do on every screen without reading instructions twice.
- 5: Each question type is clear at a glance, and the instruction is short and plain.
- 3: Some types need a second look, or instructions are long.
- 1: A learner could get stuck.

**4. Consistency.** The same things are in the same places across every question type and screen.
- 5: Prompt, answer area, chips, Continue and the answer bar sit in the same positions with the same sizes and
  spacing everywhere.
- 3: A few types break the pattern.
- 1: Each screen feels designed separately.

**5. Typography and spacing.** Type and space create a clear order of reading.
- 5: A clear type scale, French and English easy to tell apart, comfortable spacing, nothing cramped or floating.
- 3: Readable but flat, or uneven spacing.
- 1: Hard to scan.

**6. Light and dark.** Both modes are designed, not inverted.
- 5: Both read well, with matched contrast. The accent works on both backgrounds.
- 3: One mode is clearly weaker.
- 1: Text or controls are hard to read in one mode.

**7. Tone.** Words are warm and direct. Nothing childish, nothing corporate.
- 5: Feedback lines, labels and instructions sound like a calm adult. No game language (no streak pressure, no
  rewards, no "Amazing!").
- 3: Mostly right, with a few lines off.
- 1: Childish, pushy or robotic.

**8. Single bite.** The app feels light: a lesson is a small, complete piece you can finish while waiting in line.
- 5: Home makes the next lesson one tap away. The tree reads quickly. The sushi icons are consistent and calm.
- 3: Home takes some looking to find the next step.
- 1: The next step is buried.

**9. Feedback and states.** Right, wrong, typo and accent states are clear and quick.
- 5: The answer bar shows the result and the correct answer at once. Matched pairs leave smoothly. Errors are
  plain.
- 3: States are clear but slow, or inconsistent across types.
- 1: A learner can't tell whether they were right.

## Never acceptable

Any of these is a top fix, whatever the grades: hearts, chests, gems, combo counters, character interjections,
celebration screens, timers, loading spinners inside a lesson, or text that's unreadable in either mode.

## Report format

| Criterion | Grade | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |

Then: overall grade (the average, one decimal), and the fix list.

# Tamago: learning methods

Draft 1, November 7, 2026. How Tamago teaches adults, and the methods it uses beyond remediation. Each method
says where it fits in the app. IDs match the workbook. Meanings and conjugations stay out of this document; they
come from Wiktionary.

## 1. Philosophy

1. **Memory is built by pulling things out of it.** Answering from memory teaches more than reading the answer
   again. Most of a lesson is the learner producing or choosing an answer, not looking at material.
2. **Forgetting is part of the design.** An item that comes back after a gap and takes effort to recall gets
   stronger. Getting everything right in one sitting feels good and proves little.
3. **Adults can use a rule when told it.** Tell them the rule briefly, then get them practicing. Don't make them
   guess it from examples, and don't lecture.
4. **Language is sound first.** A learner who only reads French builds wrong sounds in their head. Every French
   sentence should be heard, and speaking should start early. French spelling is a poor guide to its sound, which
   makes this matter more.
5. **Help fades.** The five rounds move from recognition to recall. Each round should remove support, and the
   last round should have none.
6. **Practice has to look like use.** Translation drills build knowledge, not the ability to take part in a
   conversation. Learners also need to understand and say things for their meaning.
7. **Adults run their own learning.** They have a reason for being here and limited time. Give them a choice of
   topic and honest progress. Never use guilt, pressure or rewards as the reason to continue.
8. **Measure what lasts.** The useful number is whether something can be recalled a day or more later, not the
   score in the lesson.

## 2. Where Tamago stands now

Paul Nation's four strands are a useful check. He recommends a course give roughly equal time to each.

| Strand | What it is | Tamago now | Gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Language-focused learning | Deliberate study of words, sounds, grammar | The 10-minute lesson, grammar notes, side tools | Strong |
| Meaning-focused input | Reading and listening to understand a message | Single sentences; QT20 is planned for later | Weak |
| Meaning-focused output | Saying or writing something to communicate | QT09 only; QT21 is planned for later | Weak |
| Fluency | Using what is already known, easily and quickly | Nothing | Missing |

The lesson stays the core, and it should not grow to fill these gaps. Methods 10 to 13 add the other strands in
small pieces around it.

## 3. Methods

### Inside the lesson

**1. New-word limit.** Introduce no more than about 4 new words in a lesson, and use a sentence only when its other
words have been met. Too many new items at once means none get learned.
- *Fits:* lesson builder, round 1. Show the meaning beside a new word at first sight.
- *When:* now. In the current build, 16 to 18 of Unit 1's 18 words appear in the first round 1 lesson.

**2. Cumulative slots.** From Unit 2 on, 2 of every 10 questions come from earlier units, chosen by what is most
overdue on the FSRS schedule. Old material then returns without the learner choosing to review it. Mixing old and new
also makes the learner work out which form or rule applies, which blocked practice doesn't demand.
- *Fits:* lesson builder, rounds 2 to 5. Round 1 stays on the current unit. The research supports blocking first and
  mixing after, and a purely random mix has not always helped.
- *When:* Phase 2, as soon as Unit 2 exists.

**3. Contrast practice.** When a unit has a grammar point, make the wrong choices test it. The learner should have to
choose between un and une, or suis and es, rather than rule out an unrelated word. Learning happens when the learner
has to notice the difference.
- *Fits:* distractor rules for QT05, QT07 and QT08. Use the unit's grammar_point to choose the contrast.
- *When:* now. Today, the other article appears in only about 7% of round 3 chip questions on un or une sentences.

**4. Sound with every sentence.** Play the French when the answer bar appears, on every question type. The learner
connects spelling to sound many times with no extra screens. The audio must never hold up the next question.
- *Fits:* answer bar. Off under Can't listen now.
- *When:* now. Today, QT05, QT08 and QT12 can pass with the learner never hearing the sentence.

**5. Aloud, some of the time.** Saying a word aloud helps memory more than reading it silently. The benefit is
strongest when spoken items are mixed with silent ones, and it fades when everything is spoken. One or two spoken
items in 10 fits well.
- *Fits:* QT10 from round 1, as "say it, tap Done" with no recording. This adds almost no time and needs no microphone.
- *When:* Phase 2, with the other speaking types.

**6. Speech from memory.** Repeating a sentence just heard trains the mouth, not recall. The learner also needs to see
an English prompt, say the French from memory, then play their version beside the model. This is the practice closest
to real speech, and it stays ungraded.
- *Fits:* QT13 in round 5, with QT10 and the side-by-side comparison carrying rounds 1 to 4.
- *When:* Phase 2. Needs real recordings as the model; only 5 of 36 live sentences have one.

**7. Explain the error.** A rule can catch many errors without a model: wrong article, wrong verb form, missing word,
word order. Name the type in one short line in the answer bar and link to the unit's grammar note. Don't add an
explanation screen. Feedback that shows what went wrong helps more than a bare right or wrong.
- *Fits:* answer bar, typed and chip answers. Rule explanations come from the grammar note and Wiktionary, not model
  memory. Claude explanations join in Phase 4 as planned.
- *When:* the rule-based version in Phase 2.

### Around the lesson

**8. Spaced rounds.** Five rounds in one day gives far less than the same rounds across several days. Nothing locks.
The home screen should recommend the review that is due first, and say plainly that the next round works best
tomorrow. A learner who wants to continue can.
- *Fits:* home screen and tree. Skill strength bars show the same schedule.
- *When:* Phase 2.

**9. Relearning on separate days.** An item should leave the review bank after three correct answers on three
different days, not three in a row. A missed item also returns in the next lesson at its original difficulty, since a
correct answer on an easier re-ask shows little about recall. This is the direct follow-up to remediation.
- *Fits:* review bank exit rule; one slot in the next lesson.
- *When:* now. It's a small change to the bank, and today three review sessions in a row clear an item.

**10. Short known-word passages.** After a node's round 3, offer a few connected lines, as text and audio, built only
from words the learner has met. One comprehension question follows. This is the first time they read or hear French
as a message instead of a test item.
- *Fits:* optional item at the end of a node, outside the 10-minute block. This is a small early form of QT20. Lines
  come from checked Tatoeba sentences or are written and reviewed like other content. Generated versions come in
  content Phase 3.
- *When:* Phase 3. Unit 1's vocabulary is too small to make these interesting; start at about Unit 3.

**11. Say something true.** At the end of a unit, give a prompt the learner answers about themselves, such as a
greeting and who they are, by typing or speaking. It isn't graded. The learner sees model sentences from the unit
afterward. Producing something real shows them what they can't yet say, and that drives attention to the next lesson.
- *Fits:* unit end, tied to the can_do statements (CD03, CD04 in Unit 1). Claude can comment on it in Phase 4.
- *When:* Phase 2 without feedback from Claude.

**12. Answer real questions.** QT09 is the only lesson question that isn't translation. Any answer that truly fits the
question must be accepted, or it teaches the wrong lesson.
- *Fits:* QT09, with more pairs per unit and several accepted answers for each.
- *When:* Next after Phase 1. It needs no microphone, so it doesn't have to wait for the speaking types.

**13. Easy and quick.** Fluency comes from using known material without strain. Offer an optional run through mastered
sentences in a node: listening or reading, as many as the learner wants. No timer shows and nothing is scored, in
keeping with the no-timer rule. It earns points but no score, as repeated content already does.
- *Fits:* side tool, opened from a completed node.
- *When:* Phase 3.

**14. Hearing drills.** Short drills where the learner tells apart two similar sounds, heard from several different
voices, with immediate feedback. Perception training improves hearing and, to a smaller degree, pronunciation.
Hearing a sound from several speakers is the established way to do it.
- *Fits:* side tool using sound pairs from the current unit, under two minutes. Must use real recordings from several
  speakers (Lingua Libre). Browser speech isn't good enough here.
- *When:* Phase 3, depending on how many recordings exist. Drop it if the recordings aren't available.

**15. Short grammar notes.** One screen before a unit, as the feature list already plans. Add two things: the note can
be skipped, and it stays reachable from the answer bar when the learner needs it. Explicit teaching outperforms
implicit teaching in the research, and adults want the rule at the moment they get it wrong.
- *Fits:* unit start, answer bar link.
- *When:* Phase 2.

**16. Whole phrases first.** Teach common phrases as single units before taking them apart. The workbook already does
this with au revoir (W003). Extend it to useful phrases in each unit, so a learner can use them before knowing the
grammar inside them.
- *Fits:* the words and sentence_words tabs, as a content rule.
- *When:* from Unit 2 authoring on.

### Motivation and honest progress

**17. Can-do checks that test something.** Learners are poor judges of what they've learned, and repetition makes this
worse because material feels familiar. Tie each "I can" statement to a short task, and only tick it after the task:
hear it and understand it, or say it from memory and compare.
- *Fits:* progress page, unit end. Links to methods 6 and 11.
- *When:* Phase 2, when can_do ships.

**18. A plan, not just a goal.** Ask for the reason in the learner's own words, as already planned, and add one
when-and-where line: "After I pour my coffee, I do one lesson." If-then plans of this kind help people follow through.
The effect is smaller than first reported, but the cost here is one line of text.
- *Fits:* goal setting, home screen.
- *When:* with the planned goals feature.

**19. Expect a long start.** Habits take weeks to months to form, and a missed day doesn't undo the progress. A missed
day leads with the review due, with no message about the absence. This backs up what the feature list already says
about guilt.
- *Fits:* home screen, streak and weekly goal wording.
- *When:* Phase 2.

**20. Real choice.** Choosing a topic gives adults a reason to care about the content. Keep the choose-your-topic node
and the free ordering of branch nodes, since these are what separate a tree from a path.
- *Fits:* tree, as planned.
- *When:* Phase 3, as planned.

### Tuning

**21. Measure retention, then tune.** The attempts table already holds what's needed:
- **Delayed recall:** first-attempt correct on an item's next appearance at least one day later, by question type and
  variant. This is the main measure for deciding what stays in the mix.
- **Difficulty:** first-attempt correct per round. Keep it between about 70% and 90%. Under that, the round is too
  hard and failed lessons pile up. Over that, it isn't removing enough help. These limits are a starting rule based on
  the 7 of 10 pass mark, not a research finding.
- **Lesson time:** the gaps between answered_at values show how long a lesson takes, by round.
- **Hints:** hint taps per word, from hints_log, to find words that need more practice.

Use the variant test bank for comparisons. Dan alone can't show which variant is better. These numbers become useful
with the 5 to 10 testers.

## 4. What to leave out

- **Learning styles.** No "visual learner" settings. Matching teaching to a claimed style has weak evidence. All
  learners need sound and text.
- **Input alone.** Listening and reading alone won't produce speech. Adults also benefit from direct teaching.
- **Machine-graded pronunciation.** Tamago's rule stands. Scoring is unreliable and discourages people from speaking.
- **Speed pressure.** Fluency practice stays optional and untimed.
- **Long explanations in the lesson.** They break the 10-minute rhythm. Notes stay short and optional.
- **Rewards as the reason to continue.** This is already in the feature list; it is also the point of principle 7.

## 5. Order of work

1. **Now, small:** new-word limit (1), contrast practice (3), sound with every sentence (4), relearning on separate
   days (9).
2. **Next after Phase 1:** QT09 with real accepted answers (12).
3. **Phase 2:** cumulative slots (2), aloud (5), speech from memory (6), explaining errors (7), spaced rounds (8), say
   something true (11), grammar notes (15), can-do tasks (17), wording for missed days (19).
4. **Phase 3 and later:** passages (10), easy and quick (13), hearing drills (14), choice of topic (20).
5. **Ongoing:** whole phrases (16), measuring (21).

## 6. How firm this is

Most of this research comes from labs and classrooms, not from apps or from A1 French. It tells us the direction, not
the numbers. The limits here (4 new words, 2 cumulative slots, 70% to 90%) are starting points to tune. Three findings
are less settled than they sound:

- **Guessing before being told.** Some studies find that guessing a new word's meaning and then seeing the answer
  beats plain study, but later work limits or questions this for foreign vocabulary. So Tamago shows a new word's
  meaning at first sight instead of relying on guessing.
- **Interleaving.** It has good support for grammar and verb forms, but one study found no gain from a random or a
  simple alternating schedule. It depends on how the mix fits the task.
- **Retrieval versus restudy.** Testing beats restudy, though later work questioned how little the 2008 study found
  restudy adding. Tamago doesn't depend on that detail.

The sources below were checked to exist, and their main claims checked through abstracts or papers that cite them. The
full papers weren't read. The exception is Li (2010): the paper was confirmed, but its finding here comes from memory.

## 7. Sources

- Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks. *Psychological Bulletin*
  132. Method 8.
- Goo, Granena, Yilmaz & Novella (2015). Implicit and explicit instruction in L2 learning. In *Implicit and Explicit
  Learning of Languages*, Benjamins. Method 15.
- Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement. *Advances in Experimental Social
  Psychology* 38. Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer (2024) report smaller estimates after correcting for bias. Method 18.
- Karpicke & Roediger (2008). The critical importance of retrieval for learning. *Science* 319. Principle 1.
- Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle (2010). How are habits formed. *European Journal of Social Psychology*. Small
  sample, wide spread between people. Method 19.
- Li (2010). The effectiveness of corrective feedback in SLA. *Language Learning* 60(2). Method 7.
- MacLeod, Gopie, Hourihan, Neary & Ozubko (2010). The production effect. *Journal of Experimental Psychology:
  Learning, Memory, and Cognition* 36(3). Method 5.
- Nakata & Suzuki (2019). Mixing grammar exercises facilitates long-term retention. *The Modern Language Journal*
  103(3). Method 2.
- Nation (2007). The four strands. *Innovation in Language Learning and Teaching* 1(1). Section 2.
- Norris & Ortega (2000). Effectiveness of L2 instruction. *Language Learning* 50(3). Method 15.
- Pan, Tajran, Lovelett, Osuna & Rickard (2019). Does interleaved practice enhance foreign language learning?
  *Journal of Educational Psychology* 111(7). Method 2.
- Potts & Shanks (2014). The benefit of generating errors during learning. *Journal of Experimental Psychology:
  General*. Section 6.
- Rawson & Dunlosky (2011). Optimizing schedules of retrieval practice for durable and efficient learning.
  *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General* 140. Method 9.
- Sakai & Moorman (2018). Can perception training improve the production of second language phonemes? *Applied
  Psycholinguistics* 39(1). Method 14.
- Uchihara, Karas & Thomson (2025). High variability phonetic training: a meta-analysis of L2 perceptual training
  studies. *Studies in Second Language Acquisition*. Method 14.

# Tamago: question types and question logic

Draft 3, November 7, 2026. Updated from the learning review and its check. How a sentence becomes a question, which question
types exist, and how they phase in across the five rounds of a skill node. Table IDs match tamago-data-v5.xlsx.

## 1. The building blocks

A question is built from four parts:

| Part | What it is | Workbook tab |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Item | A sentence, or a single word, from the unit's content | sentences, words |
| Question type | What the learner does (match, build, type, listen, speak) | question_types |
| Variant | One way of doing that type | variants |
| Direction | French to English, or English to French | set per question |

One sentence feeds many questions. "Je suis une femme." can be a word match, a chip build, a typed translation,
a listening question and a spoken answer, each in a different round.

## 2. Question types

Each type trains one main skill. The skill decides which score the question feeds.

| ID | Type | Main skill | Kind | Rounds |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| QT01 | Match pairs: French words and meanings on one screen | Reading | Recognition | 1–2 |
| QT02 | Word to image | Reading | Recognition | 1–2 |
| QT03 | Pick the meaning: a French sentence, pick the English | Reading | Recognition | 1–3 |
| QT04 | Pick what you heard: audio plays, pick the English meaning (V0404) or the matching clip | Listening | Recognition | 1–3 |
| QT05 | Fill in the blank with chips | Reading | Recognition | 2–4 |
| QT06 | French to English: chips, or typed in round 5 (V0602) | Reading | Recognition to recall | 2–5 |
| QT07 | Tap what you hear: build the French with chips | Listening | Partial recall | 2–5 |
| QT08 | Build the translation, English to French, with chips | Writing | Partial recall | 3–5 |
| QT09 | Answer the question: a speaker asks, the learner answers | Writing | Partial recall | 3–5 |
| QT10 | Repeat what you hear: say it aloud. Never graded | Speaking | Imitation | 1–4 |
| QT11 | Type what you hear | Listening | Recall | 4–5 |
| QT12 | Type the translation, English to French | Writing | Recall | 4–5 |
| QT13 | Speak: imitation (V1301), or from an English prompt with no audio first (V1302). Never graded | Speaking | Recall | 4–5 |

Rounds include re-asks: a type can appear one round after its last mix round.

When Listen first hides the French, QT03 and QT06 feed Listening, not Reading.

Speaking types are never graded. They count as done when the learner says the sentence once. V1002 needs no
recording: say it, tap Done.

Later, outside the 10-minute block: QT20 listening comprehension and QT21 conversation (Phase 3, through the API).

## 3. Variants

Every type has at least one variant. All variants stay in a test bank with a status: live, testing or off.
Nothing is deleted. A variant with rounds in use_in_rounds is the only one of its type used in those rounds;
variants with it empty rotate elsewhere. Key variants:

- V0404: audio plays, pick the English meaning. Main QT04 variant in rounds 1 and 2.
- V0602: read the French, type the English. Round 5, so reading reaches recall.
- V0903: QT09 with the question written out, for Can't listen now.
- V1002: say it aloud, no recording.
- V1302: English prompt, say the French from memory, then play both. Round 5.

The full list is in the variants tab.

## 4. The five rounds

| Round | Name | Mix | Reading / Listening / Writing / Speaking |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Exposure | QT01 2, QT02 2, QT03 2, QT04 3, QT10 1 | 6 / 3 / 0 / 1 |
| 2 | Guided | QT03 1, QT04 2, QT05 2, QT06 2, QT07 2, QT10 1 | 5 / 4 / 0 / 1 |
| 3 | Build | QT05 2, QT07 2, QT08 3, QT09 1, QT10 2 | 2 / 2 / 4 / 2 |
| 4 | Partial recall | QT06 1, QT07 1, QT08 1, QT09 1, QT11 2, QT12 2, QT13 2 | 1 / 3 / 4 / 2 |
| 5 | Recall | QT06 1, QT09 2, QT11 2, QT12 3, QT13 2 | 1 / 2 / 5 / 2 |

Choices: 3 in rounds 1 and 2, 4 in round 3, none after. Round 4 has fewer chip questions, each with more
distractors. Round 2 gives QT07 one distractor chip, the contrast word.

## 5. How a lesson is put together

1. Take the node's items and the current round.
2. New words: no more than 4 per lesson. A sentence is used only when its other words have been met. In round 1,
   a sentence may appear twice in one lesson in two different types. Use the 4-pair QT01 variant (V0102) when
   fewer than 5 words are available.
3. A missed item from the last lesson fills one slot, at its original type.
4. For each item, pick a type allowed in this round that the item can support: word to image needs an image,
   listening needs audio, answer the question needs a row in qa_answers.
5. Pick a live variant, rotating so the same variant doesn't repeat back to back.
6. Distractors: at least one wrong chip is a contrast from the unit's contrast_sets (un/une, suis/es). Others
   come from the same unit, same part of speech and gender where possible.
7. No type more than 3 times, counted before swaps and fallbacks.

## 6. Answering, remediation and review

- **First sight**: a new word's meaning shows the first time. On QT01, a wrong tap on a new word isn't a miss.
- **Pass mark**: first attempts count. Speaking earns a point but isn't graded. Pass is 70% of graded
  questions, rounded up.
- **Re-asks**: a miss returns at the end of the lesson as a different type: the same round's type or one round
  easier (a missed QT12 returns as QT08). A wrong re-ask shows the answer and the lesson moves on; the item stays
  in the bank.
- **Under the pass mark**: the lesson doesn't count and restarts with the same items in new types.
- **Review bank**: misses in rounds 2 to 5 go in. Round 1 misses and hinted words don't. An item leaves after
  three correct answers on three different days.
- **Hints** never cost a strike and are always logged.
- **Points**: 1 per first-attempt correct answer or completed speaking question, shown on home only.
- **Answer bar**: the French plays on every question when the bar appears, without blocking Continue.

## 7. Answer checking (rule-based, no API in version 1)

- Normalize: lower case, trim, collapse spaces, ignore final punctuation and the space before ? and !.
- Check against the main sentence and every live accepted answer.
- QT09 accepts any answer listed for the question in qa_answers.
- Lenient by default: one-letter typo accepted on words of 3 letters or more, if the typo isn't another known
  word. Missing accent accepted at A1 and pointed out. Strict setting: no typos, accents required.

## 8. Swaps

- Can't listen now and Can't speak now swap types per the cant_swaps tab.
- Phase 1 swaps types not built yet per the phase1_fallbacks tab. Build QT09 before the speaking types.
- A swapped question feeds the replacement's skill. The swapped-out skill doesn't move.

## 9. Open items

- Name for a round ("coin" is the working word).
- Lesson time: log it by round to check whether 10 questions fills 10 minutes.
- The limits (4 new words, 70% pass) are starting numbers, to tune after use.

# Tamago: feature list

Saved November 6, 2026. Updated November 7, 2026 (learning review applied). A language-learning web app that brings back old
Duolingo's best features for serious adult learners. Dan uses it first, then opens it to others. Not a spec yet.

## Direction

- Bring back the features Duolingo removed or weakened: forums, answer flags, the word list, grammar notes.
- Built for real progress: CEFR levels instead of points, no punishments, no graded pronunciation.
- Built for adults, not children. No candy, chests, toys or cartoon pressure.
- **The 10-minute lesson is the core.** A learner opens the app in a line and finishes a lesson before it moves.
  Nearly all of the 10 minutes is questions, one after another. Speed between questions matters more than
  anything else on screen.
- Market is crowded at the top (Duolingo, Babbel, Busuu, Rosetta Stone); Busuu is the closest existing app
  (CEFR levels, native-speaker corrections). Openings: less common languages and regional variants.

## Languages

- English to French only for now, with an English interface. Built so languages swap without changing the structure.
- Later: Spanish, then German. Italian possible.
- Scope for now: A1 in French, across all four skills.

## Progress: points, score and CEFR

Three layers, each with its own job.

- **Points (XP)**: effort. Earned for answering questions. Kept loose for now. Shown in the lesson and on home.
- **Score**: learning. One score per skill (reading, writing, listening, speaking) on Duolingo's 0–160 scale,
  used as the benchmark. Score moves only for new learning: a round finished for the first time, a review
  question cleared. Repeating content already mastered earns points but no score. This is the break between
  points and learning, so a learner can't grind writing points into a writing level.
- **CEFR level**: the label that comes from the score, using Duolingo's bands. A1 is split three ways:
  0–9 very early A1, 10–19 early A1, 20–29 high A1. A2 is 30–59.
- **Intermediate layer**: A1 alone takes months. Score shows to one decimal through A1 (Reading 4.6) so it moves
  every few lessons. Exact rate is open.
- **Where it shows**: points and a short score line on home. The full picture (per-skill score, CEFR band,
  "I can" checklist, what "A1 complete" requires) lives on its own progress page, not in the main view.
- **A1 complete for a skill**: every A1 node for that skill finished through round 5, and every A1 "I can"
  statement for that skill checked.
- Note: Duolingo's score is one number per course and moves with course completion, not with a skill test.
  Per-skill score is Tamago's own addition.

## Lesson flow (core)

- A lesson is a block of about 8 to 10 questions. Pass is 70% of graded questions (speaking isn't graded).
- No more than 4 new words per lesson; a new word's meaning shows at first sight.
- **A miss is a strike, nothing more.** No hearts, no lives, no lockout.
- **Under the pass mark**: the lesson doesn't count; the learner repeats it right away with the same content in new
  formats. Nothing locks.
- **No timers** on any question.
- **Progress bar at the top** of the screen during questions.
- **No dead time**: no loading screens, no congratulation screens, no animations that hold the learner.
  The next question appears right away.
- **Remediation**: a missed question goes to the end of the block and comes back in a different question type
  (same content, new format).
- **Answer bar**: after each answer, a bar at the bottom shows right or wrong and the correct answer, and the
  French plays without blocking Continue. The flag
  and comment icons sit in this bar, bottom right, faint outlines. Correction: earlier versions of this list
  put them bottom left during the question. Nothing extra shows while the learner is answering.
  - **Flag** gives a short list of reasons (my answer should be accepted, audio is wrong, translation is wrong,
    something is broken).
  - **Comment** shows the comment count and opens that question's discussion. Stubbed in version 1; working in
    version 3.
- **Feedback lines**: the answer bar shows short, warm, direct lines that rotate ("Nice.", "Not quite."), not a
  fixed Correct or Incorrect. French lines ("Très bien !", "Presque !") rotate in at a flexible rate, about one
  per lesson to start, with tap-for-meaning. Instructions shift toward French as the course goes up in level.
- **Match pairs**: a correct pair animates out together; no green outline.
- **New word tag**: the first time a word appears, the question says so and the word is highlighted.
- **Tap a word for hints**: words with a dotted underline open a small table of translations, from Wiktionary.
  A hint never costs a strike. Every hint is logged. Correction: hinted words no longer go to review.

## Answer checking

- Default is lenient: a one-letter typo is accepted and the correct spelling is shown. Extra spaces are ignored.
  A missing accent counts as correct at A1 and is pointed out. A wrong word is a miss.
- A setting lets the learner make checking stricter.

## Review and skill strength (core, outside tree progress)

- **Review bank**: misses in rounds 2 to 5 go in (round 1 misses don't). Review draws from the bank. A question
  leaves the bank after three correct answers on three different days. Review doesn't count toward progress in the tree.
- **Skill strength**: each skill node shows four bars that drop over time without practice, on the FSRS schedule.
- **Practice weak skills**: one button on the tree pulls from the weakest skills.
- **Review checkpoints**: a review node appears in the tree after a set amount of new content. Stubbed for now.

## Question types (core)

- **Fill in the blank** with word chips at the bottom. A chip can be a whole word or part of a word.
  Variant: the blank sits inside a speaker's dialogue bubble.
- **Type the translation** from source to target language, with word chips ("chiclets") to build the answer.
  A keyboard icon in the chip bank switches to typing; a setting makes it the default.
- **Word to image match**: a word at the top, pick the matching image (tomato). Variant: the English word at the
  top, four images labeled in French.
- **Match pairs**: target words and their meanings on one screen, tap to pair them (the old Words matching).
- **Answer the question**: a speaker asks something ("How do I get to the park?") and the learner answers
  instead of translating.
- **Listening**: type what you hear, tap what you hear (word chips), pick what you heard, a slow button.
  - **Audio-only answers**: when a listening question has choices, the choices are speaker buttons, not text.
    Written French choices turn a listening question into a reading question; English meaning choices are fine.
  - Text stays hidden until the learner answers. Option to try: text appears only after the second play.
- **Repeat what you hear**: audio only, text behind a reveal button, then say it. Never graded. Starts in round 1.
- **Speak from memory**: an English prompt, say the French, then hear both. Round 5. Never graded.
- **Speaking, never graded**: listen to a native recording, record yourself, play both side by side.
- Question types work off one sentence corpus in different ways.
- **Variants**: each question type can have several ways to interact (six or more for listening, for example).
  All variants stay live in a test bank. Nothing is deleted; weak variants are kept, changed or switched off.
- **Phasing**: early lessons use fewer, simpler types and fewer choices. Types and choices grow with level.
- Later, outside the 10-minute block: **listening comprehension** (one audio scenario, then several short typed
  answers) and conversations.

## Learning tree (core)

- Organized by CEFR level (A1–C2). Each unit pairs a topic with one grammar point and one or two
  CEFR "I can" statements. Short placement check; "I can" checklist at the end of each level.
- Skills show as icons in rows of one, two or three. Locked skills are gray. Each shows a lesson count (2/7)
  and its strength bars.
- **Five rounds per skill node**: the same content five times, with less help each round.
  Round 1 is exposure (match words, recognize, pick from choices). Round 5 is recall with nothing pre-filled
  (type it from scratch). The question-type mix per round sets the scaffolding. Name for a round is open
  ("coin" is the working word).
- **Branching**: some points have one node; others open to three nodes the learner can take in any order,
  all three required before moving on. Learners can go forward only so far ahead.
- **Choose your topic**: one of the three nodes can be a pick. About 7 topics shown from a pool of about 30
  (airports, dogs, tree types, Chinese food, cloud types). The chosen topic feeds that node's questions.
- Topic packs are built from checked Tatoeba sentences and reviewed before release.
- **Grammar note** for each unit: a short screen before the lesson with the rule in plain words and two or three
  examples with audio (the old Tips, for example savoir vs. connaître).
- The question tree and the learning tree are worked on separately.

## Side tools (outside the learning tree)

- **Word list / dictionary** of every word met: how well it's known, conjugations, example sentences.
  A mini exercise to test those words, with both modes: matching (recognition) and flashcards (recall).
  Option to say each word out loud.
- **Verb conjugation trainer** with its own mini exercises.
- **Flashcards** from the word list, scheduled with FSRS.

## Settings and habits

- **Listen first**: audio plays with text hidden; text appears after answering. Those questions then feed the
  Listening score, not Reading.
- **Can't listen now / Can't speak now**: pause for 15 minutes or 1 hour, swapped for reading and typing so
  the lesson still counts; a setting turns either off permanently. A swapped question feeds the replacement's
  skill; the swapped-out skill's score doesn't move.
- **Word chips or keyboard** for typed answers.
- **Answer strictness** (see Answer checking).
- **Points and streaks** with an off switch; optional weekly goal (e.g. 4 days a week); no hearts or energy.
- **No notifications at first.** Later: goals in the learner's words (how much to practice, and why, in free
  text); reminders use that sentence; learner picks the time and email or notification, or turns them off.
  The reason shows on the home screen. No guilt after missed days.
- **Light and dark mode.**

## Platform

- One responsive web app, mobile first (most use will be on phones), with a desktop layout.
  Installable to the Home Screen.
- **Next lesson always preloaded** on the device. A lesson runs with no connection.
- Version 1 is Dan only: no sign-in, all progress on the device, nothing to sync.
- Planned for later: profile with screen name and email, authentication, then sync across devices. Screen names
  show in question comments and the forum.

## Mascot and characters

- **Mascot: a piece of tamago sushi with no face.**
- Later: animal characters as speakers in dialogue questions. Squirrels and forest creatures first, octopuses
  later. Placeholder images to start. Leave an image slot in those question layouts now.

## Content phases

- **Phase 1: baseline from free sources** (Tatoeba, Wiktionary, Lingua Libre). Fixed content, reviewed by us.
- **Phase 2: features that need more specific content**, built by us over time (topic packs, more question
  variants).
- **Phase 3: learner-guided content.** Tamago owns the framework and the data shape. The learner steers what
  gets made (a lesson on a weak point, flashcards from pasted words, a test on this week's topics, a text
  rewritten in French with questions). An LLM returns structured data that fits Tamago's question types.
  Conversations with a model happen here, through API calls.
- Note: generated sentences and questions are fine; definitions and conjugations in them still come from Wiktionary.

## Later

- **Version 2: answer flags.** "My answer should be accepted" goes to a review list; approved answers are
  accepted for everyone.
- **Version 3: sentence discussions.** A thread under each question: sentence with audio and translation,
  comment count, threaded replies with up and down votes, report link. Claude screens for spam.
- **Forum**: stub only for now. Each question's thread also lives in a Sentence Discussions section of the
  forum, so a learner can browse discussions by question without being in a lesson. An Unanswered filter.
  Other sections: threads and categories by language; Popular, New and Followed tabs.

## Left out on purpose

From current and recent Duolingo: hearts, gems, chests, Daily Quests, the Super upsell, "Jump here?" skips,
"Perfect lesson" stat screens, character interjections between questions ("5 in a row"), combo counters,
streak commitment screens, the XP nag bar, puzzle and costume events.

## Content

| What | Source | License |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sentences with translations, some audio | Tatoeba (checked sentences only) | CC BY |
| Definitions, conjugations, grammar, word hints | Wiktionary | CC BY-SA |
| Native pronunciation recordings | Lingua Libre | CC BY-SA |
| Audio for any sentence | Browser text-to-speech | Free |
| Review scheduling | FSRS | MIT |
| Grammar and vocabulary by level (Spanish) | Instituto Cervantes curriculum plan | Free online |
| Grammar and vocabulary by level (French) | To find: French equivalent of the Cervantes plan | To check |
| Images for word to image match | To find: openly licensed image set | To check |

An About the content page carries the credits. Content built from CC BY-SA sources is shared under the same license.

## Where Claude fits

- Checks typed answers and explains mistakes; writes practice sentences from known words; screens discussion posts.
- Facts (definitions, conjugations) come from Wiktionary, never the model's memory.
- A smaller, cheaper model for answer checking, with a daily limit per learner.
- Phase 3 generation (see Content phases).

## Opening it to others

- Dan first, then 5–10 testers learning the same language, then public.
- Minimum age 13; store as little personal data as possible.
- Its own name and look; nothing resembling Duolingo's name, owl or green.

## Name

**Tamago** (Japanese for egg). Mascot is faceless tamago sushi. Progress shows as plain CEFR levels.
Before committing, check the US trademark database (education and software), the domain and app store names.
"Wasabi" is already used by a Japanese language school.

## Documents to build

- **question-types.md**: question types, their variants, how each works off the corpus, and how they phase in
  across the five rounds. Dan wants Fable to take this. Vintage screenshots received November 7.
- **learning-methods.md**: learning philosophy for adults, and methods beyond remediation.
- **duolingo-2012-2017.md**: features Duolingo had and removed. Vintage screenshots received November 7.
- **unmet-needs.md**: user complaints and needs Dan pastes in, logged as they arrive. Started November 7.

## Inputs received

- **The Duolingo Handbook (2025)**: principles that explain the changes Tamago reacts to.
  - The Tree was replaced by the linear Path in 2022. Tamago keeps a tree with choice.
  - Characters are named as Duolingo's moat against AI learning tools. Tamago competes on the learning.
  - Hearts and ad removal drive the paid plan. Tamago has no hearts.
  - Their own handbook says learning outcomes are hard to measure. Tamago uses CEFR per skill as the measure.
  - Useful to keep: "clock speed" applied to time between questions.
- **Current Duolingo desktop, dark mode (November 2026)**: Path, chests, gems, hearts, Super upsell, Daily Quests.
- **X thread of Claude prompts for French learners (November 2026)**: source of the Phase 3 ideas.
- **Vintage Duolingo screenshots (November 7)**: the old tree with strength bars and Practice Weak Skills,
  question types, the answer bar with flag and discuss icons, sentence discussions, the language forums,
  Tips, Can't speak now, the streak calendar.
- **Duolingo Score (Wikipedia, duoplanet)**: 0–160 scale with CEFR bands; score rises as course content is
  completed; French reaches 130. Also from Wikipedia: volunteer course contributors ended March 2021;
  community forums shut down March 2022.

# Tamago: the model story

November 10, 2026. Which AI does what in Tamago, under which rules, and how each one is checked. Drafted from the
project's own documents (feature list, autonomous build brief, craft review, check-in) and from the code as built.
Where something isn't in place yet, it says so.

## Tamago's product rules

These hold for every AI below, and for the app itself.

- **The 10-minute lesson is the core.** A learner opens the app in a queue and finishes a lesson before the queue
  moves. Nearly all of those 10 minutes are questions, one after another. Nothing may slow the step from one
  question to the next: no loading spinners inside a lesson, no screens to click through.
- **No game rewards.** No hearts, chests, gems, combo counters, character interjections, celebration screens or
  timers. Points and streaks are quiet indicators, and a setting turns them off.
- **Facts come from Wiktionary.** Word meanings, hints and verb tables come from Wiktionary (CC BY-SA), never from
  a model's memory. Sentences come from Tatoeba wherever possible; any sentence written for Tamago is marked as
  such and waits for a native speaker's check.
- **A native speaker, not an AI, checks the French** Tamago wrote itself. No model does this step.

## 1. The builder

- **Purpose:** builds and maintains the app and its content: code, the content pipeline, the workbook, tests,
  the build log and the daily check-in for Dan.
- **Model:** Claude, working in Claude Code (currently Claude Opus 5.5).
- **Rules it follows:** the autonomous build brief (`_source/autonomous-build.md`) and the project notes
  (`CLAUDE.md`). It works phase by phase, tests, commits and pushes at each step, and logs every decision. It stops
  and waits for Dan for anything that costs money or needs an account, for making anything public or opening it to
  testers, for deleting Dan's files, and for the native-speaker check.
- **Where its facts must come from:** Tatoeba for sentences, Wiktionary for meanings and conjugations, Lingua Libre
  for recordings, the CEFR self-assessment grid for "I can" statements. When Tatoeba has nothing that fits, it may
  draft a sentence within the unit's words, marked "tamago_original" and listed for the native check.
- **Must never:** state a definition or conjugation from memory; add game rewards; put spinners in a lesson; open
  the app to testers or spend money on its own; put keys or secrets in the app or the documents.
- **Cost limits:** none inside the app. It runs under Dan's Claude Code account, and Dan decides when it works.
- **How it's graded:** the automated tests (unit tests for the lesson engine, answer checking and content rules;
  browser runs in Chrome and Firefox), the content check (every live sentence and word matched against Tatoeba and
  Wiktionary, or the build fails), an accessibility audit against WCAG 2.2 AA, the craft review below, and Dan's
  own test notes.

## 2. The reviewer

- **Purpose:** grades how the app looks and feels, as a new learner would meet it. It doesn't judge the French or
  the learning logic.
- **Model:** a separate Claude Code session that didn't build Tamago, so it comes without the builder's
  assumptions.
- **Rules it follows:** the craft review rubric (`_source/craft-review.md`): use the live site as a new learner,
  screenshot every screen and state, time the lesson, grade nine criteria from 1 to 5 with one line of evidence
  each, and list fixes in order. It changes no code.
- **Where its facts must come from:** what it sees and measures on the live site, with a screenshot named for each
  grade.
- **Must never:** change code or content; grade from the code instead of the screen; round a grade up. When in
  doubt between two grades, it gives the lower one.
- **Cost limits:** none inside the app; it runs when Dan asks for a review.
- **How it's graded:** Dan reads the review against the screenshots. Anything on the rubric's "never acceptable"
  list is a top fix whatever the grades.

## 3. Mistake explanations ("Why?")

- **Purpose:** after a wrong typed answer, one or two plain sentences on what differs from the closest accepted
  answer, and why it matters.
- **Model:** Claude Haiku 5.5, a smaller, faster model (the feature list asks for a smaller, cheaper model for
  answer checking), at low effort.
- **Rules it follows:** answer only from what the app sends: the exercise, the learner's answer, the accepted
  answers, and the Wiktionary meanings of the sentence's words. No greeting, no praise, no exclamation marks, no
  lists. If the reason can't be told from what it was given, it just names the difference.
- **Where its facts must come from:** only that message. It never adds meanings or verb forms of its own.
- **Must never:** define words or give conjugations beyond what it was sent; slow the lesson. The request goes out
  in the background, and the Why? link appears only once an explanation has arrived. Continue never waits for it.
- **Cost limits:** 30 explanations a day per device; up to 2,000 output tokens per explanation; a key used only by
  Tamago, in its own Anthropic workspace with a $5 monthly spend limit. One explanation costs a fraction of a cent.
  Requests from other sites are refused.
- **How it's graded:** not yet systematically. Learners can flag an answer, and Dan reviews flags. A set of known
  mistakes with expected explanations, scored the same way each time, is the next step.

## 4. The practice writer (Self-Study, "Written by Claude")

- **Purpose:** writes fresh practice from the words a learner has already met: short sentences to translate, and
  short two-person listening exchanges with three comprehension questions.
- **Model:** Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort, with the platform's fallback to another model if it's busy. It returns
  structured data in a fixed shape, so the app can check every line.
- **Rules it follows:** use only the French words in the list it's given, in the forms listed, and only the names
  listed; keep sentences short, natural and literal; give plain, faithful English.
- **Where its facts must come from:** the learner's own met words, with their Wiktionary meanings. The app then
  re-splits every French line against its word list and drops any line with a word outside it, so a meaning can
  never come from the model.
- **Must never:** introduce a word the learner hasn't met; write idioms; feed the score, the review bank or the
  learner's memory schedule. Its sessions are kept apart from progress.
- **Cost limits:** at most 8 sentences per request; at most 150 words sent; up to 8,000 output tokens; the same
  Tamago-only key and $5 monthly workspace limit. There's no per-device daily cap yet, so the workspace limit is
  the ceiling.
- **How it's graded:** the app's own filter (any line with an unmet word is dropped; if fewer than three
  sentences survive, the learner is asked to try again) and the unit tests for that filter. Its French isn't
  checked by a native speaker, and the screen says so.

## 5. The conversation partner (scenes on the path, partner in Self-Study)

- **Purpose:** a short spoken or typed conversation in the course language. Scenes (three per course, after the
  second help circle) speak a little above the learner's level on purpose, so asking for help is the practice. The
  partner in Self-Study follows the learner's filters: topic, vocabulary (my words only, or plus a few new), speed
  (slow, normal, natural), corrections (each turn, at the end, or off).
- **Model:** Claude Haiku 5.5, the small, low-cost model, at low effort. It returns each line in a fixed shape (the
  line, an English translation shown only on request, an optional correction, and whether the scene is over). The
  system prompt and word lists stay the same for a whole conversation, so they are cached after the first turn.
- **Rules it follows:** speak only the course language, even when explaining; short lines, one question at a time;
  use the learner's met words (scenes add one or two A1 words a line on purpose; the partner's "plus a few new"
  allows one now and then); answer every help phrase properly in the course language: slow down, repeat word for
  word, rephrase more simply, explain a word with simpler words, give the word asked for, or guess the word being
  described. No grading, no lavish praise, no emoji or markdown.
- **Where its facts must come from:** for what it says, the conversation itself. For meanings, never from it: the
  app splits each line with the content pipeline's own splitter, and a course word's meaning and picture come from
  Tamago's Wiktionary data. Only course words go to the Glossary and Review at the end.
- **Must never:** speak English to the learner; grade; lecture; feed scores or the review bank (new course words
  join the Glossary and a flashcard review the learner chooses).
- **Cost limits:** 14 learner turns per conversation (help taps count), enforced on the server too; 240 characters a
  line; 400 words sent per list; up to 1,500 output tokens a turn; the same Tamago-only key and $5 monthly workspace
  limit. A whole conversation costs well under a cent.
- **How it's graded:** not yet. The help phrases are the thing to check: for each, does Claude slow down, repeat,
  rephrase or explain in the course language? A fixed set of scripted conversations, one per help phrase per course,
  scored the same way each time, is the next step. Its lines aren't checked by a native speaker, and nothing it says
  becomes course content.

## When something goes wrong

- A learner flags a question or an answer; Dan reviews the flags, and accepted answers fold into the content.
- If the key lapses or the monthly cap is reached, all three Claude
  features switch off quietly and the rest of the app works as before.

# The full test suite after every push to main (Dan, 2026-11-16, tiered testing). Before a push, the pre-push hook
# runs the fast tier (npm run test:fast: logic tests, full sweeps for the courses that changed, a 5% sample of the
# rest) with the smoke, audio-stop and secrets checks. Here the whole suite runs: every course swept in full. A failure
# marks the run red on GitHub and emails the person who pushed; fix it in the next push. It doesn't hold the deploy:
# Cloudflare builds from the push as before.
name: Full suite
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
concurrency:
  group: full-suite-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45
    env:
      PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD: '1'
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
